extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical geometry / historians of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Using Archimedes' 'mechanical method' to determine volumes and centres of gravity of solids by comparing corresponding plane sections, imagining balances, and reducing to known results (cones, cylinders, paraboloids, spheres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare corresponding plane sections perpendicular to the axis
rubrics_metrics.description: A plane drawn at right angles to the axis cuts the solids (cylinder, spheroid/paraboloid/segment of sphere, cone) in corresponding circles or parallelograms (e.g. "it will cut the cylinder in a circle with diameter MN, the spheroid in a circle with diameter OP, and the cone in a circle with diameter QR").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the mechanical method, identify a family of parallel planes perpendicular to the axis; compute the radii/diameters of the sections using geometric relations (ordinates, generators) and use these corresponding sections as elemental masses to compare solids. Repeat "for all the circles making up" the solids to pass from element-wise balance to whole-solid balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-wise equilibrium (balance) about a point
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a single section (circle/parallelogram/triangle) of one solid is "in equilibrium, about A, with" one or more sections of other solids when those other sections are imagined to have their centres of gravity at a chosen point (e.g. "the circle in the cylinder ... is in equilibrium, about A, with the circle in the spheroid and the circle in the cone together, if both the latter circles are placed with their centres of gravity at H").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distances from the chosen fulcrum and areas (or moments) of the sections to establish equilibrium for each corresponding triple/pair of sections; this is the local step which, when summed over all sections, yields the global result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate (sum) section balances to infer whole-solid equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: If corresponding sections balance for every plane in the family, then "taking all the circles which fill up" the solids shows the whole solids are in equilibrium about the same point (e.g. "if we take all the circles making up the whole cylinder and the whole segment and treat them in the same way, we find that the cylinder ... is in equilibrium about A with the segment placed with its centre of gravity at H").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage from element-wise to whole-solid relies on treating the solids as made up of infinitesimal (or many) parallel sections; explicitly state that the sets of sections 'make up' the solids and sum their moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a thought-experiment balance (extend axis to H with HA = AD etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagine an extended axis or a bar of a balance with a middle point at A by producing the axis to H and making specified equalities (e.g. "Produce DA, the axis of the segment, to H, making HA equal to AD. Imagine that HD is the bar of a balance, A being its middle point.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device fixes a fulcrum and reference distances; construct it in the figure and place the centres of gravity of auxiliary pieces at H to compute moments. Always state the chosen equalities (HA = AD, HA = AC, etc.) used to locate H.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate mass/volume ratios to distances along the axis (moment relation HA:AK = mass ratios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ratios of segments on the extended axis in terms of ratios of whole solids, using the equilibrium relation (e.g. "HA : AK = (cylinder) : (segment)").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After proving equilibrium, use the fact that K (centre of gravity of one piece) and H (placement of the other) are points on the balance bar; then HA:AK equals the ratio of the masses (volumes) placed at those points. This yields the desired proportion between solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use known Euclidean propositions and prior results
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite and apply classical results (e.g. "cylinder = 3 (cone ALF); [Eucl. x11. 10]") and previously proven propositions in reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible reduce the new theorem to previously established ratios or Euclid results; explicitly name or cite the reference used so the chain of reasoning is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit conic-section properties to relate ordinates and radii
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the defining metric relations of conics (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola) to relate straight-line segments and squared ordinates that determine section diameters (e.g. "by the property of the parabola, DA:AS = BD^2 = OS^2").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive expressions for the radii/diameters of cross-sections in terms of ordinates/generators, then substitute into area or moment comparisons. Explicitly state the conic property used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct auxiliary solids (cones, cylinders) with same base & axis to compare with given segment
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given segment of a solid (paraboloid, sphere, etc.), construct a cone and/or cylinder that shares the same base and axis, and use those simpler solids as comparators (e.g. "imagine (1) a cone drawn with the latter circle as base and A as vertex, and (2) a cylinder with the same circle as base and AD as axis").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing simple comparator solids with known centres of gravity and volume relations lets you transfer results via section-wise balancing; explicitly describe those comparator constructions in the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use known centres of gravity of simple solids (cones, cylinders, semicircles, hemisphere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established positions of centroids (e.g. "the centre of gravity of the cone is at a point V such that AG = 4 GV", "centre of gravity of hemisphere divides axis in the ratio 5:3").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these known centroid locations when placing comparator solids at H and computing moments. Quote or re-derive the centroid facts being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate equalities of sums of squared segments into area/volume relations (circles/parallelograms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert algebraic relations involving sums of squares of lengths into equalities of areas of circles or parallelograms (e.g. (OP^2 + QR^2) corresponds to (circle, diam. OP + circle, diam. QR)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the text writes expressions like "(SO'^2 + SQ'^2) = SQ·SM" translate the resulting lengths-squared relations into equalities of elemental areas to compare moments; keep the same units (areas for circles) in integrand-like sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose solids into elemental parallelograms/triangles/circles for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat solids as being composed of many elemental sections (parallelograms, triangles, circles) produced by planes; compare corresponding elements between solids (e.g. parallelograms in half cylinder vs. portion of cylinder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give an explicit element type and show how each element in one solid corresponds to one in the other. Use these element correspondences to form global proportions by summation (method of exhaustion / integral idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce an auxiliary curve (parabola) to reduce a solid problem to a known quadrature
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce an auxiliary parabola (or other curve) in a section so that element ratios reduce the solid's volume comparison to the quadrature of a parabolic segment (e.g. "In the semicircle HFG describe the parabola ... This reduces the portion of the cylinder problem to the known quadrature of the parabola").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the auxiliary curve so that ratios of element bases reduce to squared-ratios amenable to known area results; explain why the chosen parabola yields proportional relationships (parameters, focal/axis choices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use method of exhaustion: inscribe/circumscribe element-prisms to bound volume arbitrarily closely
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct inscribed and circumscribed solids (made of element-prisms) such that the circumscribed exceeds the inscribed by less than any assigned magnitude, and use this to deduce equalities of volumes (e.g. Prop. 14 reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how to refine the partition (make element-prisms small) so that the difference tends to zero; set up inequalities leading to contradictions under alternative assumptions (> or <) and thereby conclude equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reductio ad absurdum with element-wise proportional comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the contrary inequality of volumes (e.g. portion of cylinder > 2 × prism) and derive impossible inequalities by comparing sums of element-prisms and corresponding rectangles in the auxiliary curve construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully map element-prism ratios to element-rectangle ratios for the auxiliary planar problem, then use known equalities (e.g. rectangle GD = 3 × parabolic segment) to obtain contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply compositional ratio manipulations (ex aequali, componendo, invertendo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine and manipulate proportions by standard Euclidean moves (ex aequali, componendo, invertendo, dividendo) to pass from ratios of elements to ratios of solids (used repeatedly: "therefore, ex aequali,").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining proportions, state the rule used (ex aequali, componendo, etc.) and show the algebraic step so the inference from element proportions to whole-volume proportions is transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symmetry and choose natural coordinate/section planes to simplify relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Select planes through the axis and perpendicular planes aligned with diameters or generators (e.g. "let a sphere be cut by a plane through its centre in the circle ABCD; let AC, BD be perpendicular diameters"), exploiting symmetry to simplify section geometry and centroid positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry to reduce the number of distinct cases and ensure that centres of gravity lie on axes; explicitly call out perpendicular diameters or bisectors used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place corresponding elements' centres of gravity at a single point to compare combined effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When showing e.g. that two elements together balance a third, imagine each of the two elements moved so that their centres of gravity coincide at H, then compute combined moment vs the third (e.g. "both the latter circles are placed with their centres of gravity at H").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device simplifies the combination of multiple elements' moments into a single resultant located at the chosen point; state clearly which centres are being moved and the justification that moving an element without altering its intrinsic moment about A is permissible in the thought experiment.
